title: Accessing and Analyzing UK Road Crash Data with stats19
text:
What is STATS19 Data?

The canonical record of road traffic collisions resulting in personal injury reported to police forces in Great Britain.
High analytical potential for:

Transport planning & active travel safety.
Criminology & road traffic offense interactions.
Spatial-temporal pattern analysis.








Relational Data Structure


STATS19 consists of 3 interlinked tables linked by accident_index / collision_index: 1. Accidents / Crashes: Spatial location, timing, severity, weather, road conditions. 2. Casualties: Individual outcome, age, sex, mode of travel, severity. 3. Vehicles: Vehicle type, maneuvering, driver demographics.

title: Accessing and Analyzing UK Road Crash Data with stats19
text:
Why the {stats19} R Package?
Historical Challenges:

Messy annual zip files with changing column names and codings.
Manual downloading, unzipping, cleaning, and linking across years.

{stats19} Solutions:

One-line functions to download, clean, and format data.
Standardized schemas across historical data releases.
Native sf integration for spatial analysis.

library(stats19)
library(sf)
library(dplyr)

title: Accessing and Analyzing UK Road Crash Data with stats19
text:
Rapid Data Retrieval
# Download crash data for a specific year
crashes_2022 <- get_stats19(year = 2022, type = "crash")

# Format into spatial sf object
crashes_sf <- format_sf(crashes_2022)

# Download casualties and vehicles linked to crashes
casualties_2022 <- get_stats19(year = 2022, type = "casualty")
vehicles_2022   <- get_stats19(year = 2022, type = "vehicle")

Casualties over time

library(stats19)

Data provided under OGL v3.0. Cite the source and link to:

library(tidyverse)

── Attaching core tidyverse packages ──────────────────────── tidyverse 2.0.0 ──
✔ dplyr     1.2.1     ✔ readr     2.2.0
✔ forcats   1.0.1     ✔ stringr   1.6.0

✖ dplyr::lag()    masks stats::lag()
ℹ Use the conflicted package (<http://conflicted.r-lib.org/>) to force all conflicts to become errors

library(readr)


# Read pre-aggregated casualty data (built from raw STATS19 by build-data.R)
casualties_by_year_type <- read_csv("data/casualties_by_year_type.csv",
                                    show_col_types = FALSE)


# Absolute casualties over time
ggplot(casualties_by_year_type, aes(x = collision_year, y = n, color = type)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Number of casualties", color = "Type") +
  theme_minimal()









# Indexed plot (1979 = 100)
collisions_1979 <- casualties_by_year_type |>
  filter(collision_year == 1979) |>
  select(type, n) |>
  rename(n_1979 = n)

casualties_by_year_type |>
  left_join(collisions_1979, by = "type") |>
  mutate(n_indexed = n / n_1979 * 100) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = collision_year, y = n_indexed, color = type)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Casualties indexed (1979 = 100)", color = "Type") +
  theme_minimal()

title: Cars and Crime Symposium Workshop
section: Car harms: How has the burden shifted?
text:
Car harms: How has the burden shifted?
The three plots below illustrate how “car harms” have evolved differently for people driving, walking, and cycling.

Car occupant casualties — safety technology at work
Car occupant casualties have fallen dramatically since 1979, driven by seatbelt laws, airbags, crumple zones, and improved vehicle design.

casualties_by_year_type |>
  filter(type == "Car occupant") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = collision_year, y = n)) +
  geom_line(color = "#1F78B4", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(color = "#1F78B4", size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Car occupant casualties",
       subtitle = "Dramatic decline as vehicle safety improves") +
  theme_minimal()










Pedestrian casualties — harm to people walking
While car occupants have become dramatically safer, pedestrian casualties have also declined — but not nearly as steeply, and from a much higher baseline per trip.

casualties_by_year_type |>
  filter(type == "Pedestrian") |>
  ggplot(aes(x = collision_year, y = n)) +
  geom_line(color = "#E7298A", linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(color = "#E7298A", size = 2) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Pedestrian casualties",
       subtitle = "Slower progress for people outside cars") +
  theme_minimal()










Risk shift: vulnerable road user casualties per car occupant
This ratio tells the story: for every car occupant casualty, how many pedestrians and cyclists are hurt? A rising ratio means the burden of risk has shifted from people inside cars to people outside them.

ratio_data <- casualties_by_year_type |>
  filter(type %in% c("Car occupant", "Pedestrian", "Cyclist")) |>
  pivot_wider(names_from = type, values_from = n) |>
  mutate(
    ped_per_car = Pedestrian / `Car occupant`,
    cycle_per_car = Cyclist / `Car occupant`
  )

ggplot(ratio_data, aes(x = collision_year)) +
  geom_line(aes(y = ped_per_car, color = "Pedestrians per car occupant"), linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(aes(y = ped_per_car, color = "Pedestrians per car occupant"), size = 2) +
  geom_line(aes(y = cycle_per_car, color = "Cyclists per car occupant"), linewidth = 1.2) +
  geom_point(aes(y = cycle_per_car, color = "Cyclists per car occupant"), size = 2) +
  scale_color_manual(values = c("Pedestrians per car occupant" = "#E7298A",
                                 "Cyclists per car occupant" = "#66A61E")) +
  labs(x = "Year", y = "Casualty ratio",
       color = NULL,
       subtitle = "Risk burden has shifted from car occupants to vulnerable road users") +
  theme_minimal()
